Question: Why does the sky appear blue? Answer in one clear short paragraph:
The sky appears blue because of a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. When sunlight enters the Earth's atmosphere, it is made up of different wavelengths of light, including ultraviolet, visible light, and infrared radiation. The shorter wavelengths, such as ultraviolet and visible light, are scattered more easily by air molecules than the longer wavelengths, like infrared radiation. This scattering causes the sky to appear blue during the day. At sunrise and sunset, the light has to travel through more of the atmosphere's atmosphere before reaching your eyes. As a result, the blue light is scattered more than the red light, which is why the sky looks blue. In addition, the sky is bluer when the sun is higher in the sky (when there is less atmosphere for the light to pass through), so the sky is bluer when the sun is higher in the sky. So, if you look at the sky at noon, it will be bluer than if you look at the same part of the sky at sunset. But the sky is bluer at sunset because the sun is lower in the sky and the light has to travel through more of the atmosphere, so more of the blue light is scattered out of the beam that reaches your eyes.
